title: Grace at meals
tomorrow: they ran to pray, and the Prophet told them to slow down. why?

lines: THE EARTH HATH HE GIVEN TO MEN.
cards: Before the first bite, one phone comes out to photograph the plate. At the next table, heads bow for a blessing. The rabbis of the Talmud noticed two psalms that seem to argue over the plate.

One says: "The earth is the LORD's, and the fulness thereof." The other says: "The heaven, even the heavens, are the LORD's: but the earth hath he given to the children of men." So whose is the bread in front of you?

teach.b: Let both verses speak. The first view: everything is God's, all of it, so eating without a word is like helping yourself at someone else's table. The second view: the earth was given to people.
We planted, harvested, paid and cooked; the food arrived because human hands made it arrive. Both have a real case, and the Talmud throws neither out.
Rabbi Levi's answer: the first verse is before the blessing, the second is after. Before you bless, the food is God's.

teach.h: BLESS IT, AND IT'S GIVEN TO YOU.
teach.b: Once you've said the blessing, it's been given to you. The Talmud goes further: to enjoy anything in this world without a blessing is like making personal use of something holy.

That's the teaching, and it's why Jewish practice sets a short blessing before eating: over bread, thanks to God who brings forth bread from the earth, with other blessings for fruit, for wine, for what grows from the ground.

And the Torah itself asks for thanks after the meal: "When thou hast eaten and art full, then thou shalt bless the LORD thy God." So both ends of the meal are marked. Notice what the blessing does in Rabbi Levi's answer.

It doesn't make the food holy; it already belonged to God. It changes whose hands it's in: a gift held out becomes a gift received. On your own path, the pause before eating can carry that, with its source named.

how: Jewish practice sets a short blessing before eating, different for bread, fruit, wine and other foods, and Birkat Hamazon, the grace after meals; Christian graces and the Muslim bismillah are their own ways of thanking God at the table.

games.q: your friend skips grace: 'it's my food. i bought it, i cooked it.' what's the strongest case for her side, from the Talmud's own verses?
o: Psalm 115: 'the earth hath he given to the children of men.'
Psalm 24: 'the earth is the LORD's, and the fulness thereof.'
the Torah only asks for thanks on holidays, not at ordinary meals.
games.why: her side has a verse too. Rabbi Levi keeps both: the food is God's before the blessing and given to us after it.

practice: If something to eat or drink is nearby, hold it a moment before the first bite or sip, smell it, and trace it back: who grew it, who carried it, who made it.
If you pray, you can say a blessing from your own tradition; if not, a quiet thank you to all those hands is enough.
